- If sentiment history shows strong bullish signals (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; apply downward bias correction.
- If model shows steep upward trend after a spike (e.g., >85.5), true outcome often corrects sharply downward — cap forecast slope after 3–5 consecutive rising days.
- When official supply net is negative and bearish sentiment dominates, model overestimates mean; reduce forecast by 1–2% per 10% bearish sentiment weight.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows sharp decline (e.g., >10% drop from forecast), assume lagged event impact — adjust downward by 1–3% for each day of lag.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates >5% from model, check sentiment history: if sentiment is mixed or bearish, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per 0.10 drop in sentiment average.
- If multiple consecutive forecasts show similar overestimation (e.g., 3+ days), apply “mean reversion” rule: subtract 0.5–1.0% from forecast for next period if no new bullish event.
- When policy_count > 0, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% per policy event to account for regulatory headwinds.
- If recent auction supply events are frequent (e.g., 3+ auctions/30d), model tends to overreact — reduce forecast by 0.3–0.7% per auction event.
